title: Слово о пълку Игоревѣ
part: V — Svyatoslav's dream & the Golden Word
draftNote: Part V — Grand Prince Svyatoslav III wakes in Kiev from a troubled, omen-laden dream; his boyars interpret it for him as the capture of his nephews Igor and Vsevolod (the two falcons, the two young moons going dark), while the Goth women of the Crimean coast are already singing in triumph over Rus'; the movement closes with the opening of Svyatoslav's «золото слово» (Golden Word), his reproach to Igor and Vsevolod for seeking glory too soon and too rashly, still in progress as the part ends.
source: Text: editio princeps — «Ироическая пѣснь о походѣ на половцовъ удѣльнаго князя Новагорода-Сѣверскаго Игоря Святославича», ed. A. I. Musin-Pushkin, Moscow, 1800 (public domain); via Russian Wikisource. 1800 orthography preserved. Prose sense-units at the edition's punctuation (no imposed verse lineation). Transliteration: scholarly Slavist romanization (ž š č c x; ě = ѣ; ŭ / ĭ = ъ / ь). Pronunciation: reconstructed late-12th-c. Old East Slavic (see slovo-audio doc); ж/ш/ц read hard by convention. Translations made fresh from the 1800 original.
about: Grand Prince Svyatoslav III of Kiev dreams a dream thick with funerary and ill-boding imagery — black cloth, blended wine, scattered pearls, a roof stripped of its ridge-beam, ravens crying over a ravine, his tower's golden roof-planks gone — and his boyars read it to him as Igor's and Vsevolod's capture: the two princes are the two falcons whose wings the Polovtsians have clipped, and the two young moons — named Oleg and Svyatoslav, their identity beyond Igor and Vsevolod themselves uncertain — gone dark alongside two failing suns. Already, the boyars report, the Gothic maidens of the Crimean coast are singing their people's old vengeance-song against the Rus', gloating in Rus' gold, over the defeat of Igor and, a generation before, of the khan Sharukan by Vladimir Monomakh — a defeat now avenged on Sharukan's own kin. Svyatoslav then speaks his «золото слово, слезами смѣшено» (Golden Word mixed with tears), opening his reproach to his nephews for making war on the Polovtsians too early and for their own glory rather than in concert with him — a speech the poem carries into part 6. The passage is one of the densest clusters of genuine 'dark places' in the whole poem — the wording of the dream-images, the corrupt «и не сошлю», the identity of Бусъ and of the two young moons named Oleg and Svyatoslav — and no reading here claims more certainty than the single surviving 1800 print, taken from a manuscript that burned in 1812, actually supports.

sentences.t: А Святъславь мутенъ сонъ видѣ: въ Кіевѣ на горахъ си ночь съ вечера одѣвахъте мя, рече, чръною паполомою, на кроваты тисовѣ.
sentences.tr: A Svjatŭslavĭ mutenŭ sonŭ vidě: vŭ Kievě na goraxŭ si nočĭ sŭ večera oděvaxŭte mja, reče, črŭnoju papolomoju, na krovaty tisově.
sentences.l: And Svyatoslav saw a troubled dream: ‘In Kiev, on the hills, this night, from evening on, you dressed me,’ he said, ‘with a black pall, on a bed of yew.’
sentences.i: And Svyatoslav dreamed a troubled dream: ‘In Kiev, on the hills, this very night, from evening on,’ he said, ‘you were dressing me in a black funeral pall, upon a bed of yew.’
sentences.n: мутенъ сонъ, 'a troubled/turbid dream,' opens Svyatoslav's own account of the ominous dream that gives this part its name — the historical Svyatoslav III Vsevolodovich, Grand Prince of Kiev (a kinsman of Igor's, senior in the princely hierarchy), whose 'Golden Word' this whole passage builds toward. видѣ and рече are aorists ('saw,' 'said'). одѣвахъте is a genuine grammatical puzzle: the sense wants an unnamed 'they' dressing Svyatoslav (a 3rd person plural imperfect, which would ordinarily be одѣвахуть), but the 1800 print's -хъте does not cleanly match any standard verb ending; we keep it exactly as printed rather than silently emending it. чръною паполомою, 'with a black pall,' and кроваты тисовѣ, 'a bed of yew,' are both funerary images — паполома is elsewhere in the poem the shroud laid over the slain Prince Boris (part 3), and yew is traditionally associated with death and burial — so the dream announces its own dark meaning from its very first line.

sentences.t: Чрълахуть ми синее вино съ трудомь смѣшено; сыпахутьми тъщими тулы поганыхъ тльковинъ великый женчюгь на лоно, и нѣгуютъ мя; уже дьскы безъ кнѣса вмоемъ теремѣ златовръсѣмъ.
sentences.tr: Črŭlaxutĭ mi sinee vino sŭ trudomĭ směšeno; sypaxutĭmi tŭščimi tuly poganyxŭ tlĭkovinŭ velikyj ženčjugĭ na lono, i něgujutŭ mja; uže dĭsky bezŭ kněsa vmoemŭ teremě zlatovrŭsěmŭ.
sentences.l: ‘They poured me blue wine mixed with sorrow; they poured out for me, from the empty quivers of the pagan foreigners, great pearl onto my lap, and they make much of me; already the boards are without the roof-ridge in my golden-topped tower.’
sentences.i: ‘They poured me dark wine mixed with grief; from the empty quivers of pagan strangers they showered great pearls into my lap and made much of me; and already the roof-boards of my golden-crested tower have lost their ridge-beam.’
sentences.n: синее вино, 'blue/dark wine,' mixed with 'sorrow' (трудомь) keeps the dream's funereal cast — a drink of grief, not celebration. тльковинъ (поганыхъ тльковинъ) is usually glossed 'foreigners, aliens' (built on тълкъ, 'interpretation,' cf. modern толковать 'to interpret' — people whose speech must be interpreted); whether the poet means the Polovtsians specifically or foreign peoples generally is not certain. женчюгь ('pearl,' a variant spelling of жемчугъ) poured into Svyatoslav's lap is often connected — on the strength of a widespread Slavic folk-belief that to dream of pearls forecasts tears — to the dream's grief, though the poem itself never states this equivalence and the reading rests on that outside folk association, not the text. «дьскы безъ кнѣса», 'the boards without the roof-ridge [the central roof-beam or king-post]' in his 'golden-crested tower,' is one of the poem's most famous dark places, almost universally read as an omen of the roof caving in — his house or line losing its central support — though its exact image and full symbolic weight remain genuinely debated; we do not resolve it further than that. вмоемъ is printed in the 1800 edition as one run-together word (въ + моемъ, 'in my'); we keep the print's spacing rather than inserting the expected space.

sentences.t: Всю нощь съ вечера босуви врани възграяху, у Плѣсньска на болони бѣша дебрь Кисаню, и не сошлю къ синему морю.
sentences.tr: Vsju noščĭ sŭ večera bosuvi vrani vŭzgrajaxu, u Plěsnĭska na boloni běša debrĭ Kisanju, i ne sošlju kŭ sinemu morju.
sentences.l: All night, from evening on, dun ravens cawed; at Plesnensk, on the meadow, there was the ravine of Kisanya, and — I will not send — to the blue sea.
sentences.i: All night, from evening on, dun ravens croaked their omen; at Plesnensk, on the meadow by the walls, lay the ravine of Kisanya, and [they] were borne off to the blue sea.
sentences.n: босуви (бусови) врани, 'dun/grey ravens' — or possibly 'Bus's ravens,' reading босуви as a possessive tied to the same obscure Бусъ/Бусово named later in this part (unit 10); which reading is correct is not settled, and we flag it rather than choose. Плѣсньска (Plesnensk) is an old town, its exact location debated (often placed in the Galician lands); дебрь Кисаню, 'the ravine of Kisanya,' names an otherwise unattested place — genuinely obscure, like Троянь elsewhere in the poem. «и не сошлю къ синему морю» is itself one of the passage's harder textual problems: as printed, сошлю is a first-person future ('I will not send'), which does not fit the surrounding third-person narration at all; the standard scholarly move is to read this as a corruption of несошася, '[they/it] were borne, carried off' (to the blue sea). We keep the 1800 print exactly as it stands in t and give that widely proposed emendation only as the usual way past a genuine crux, not as a silent correction to the text itself. бѣша, an old plural form, is glossed here as governing the singular дебрь impersonally, but it could as plausibly be read with the earlier plural врани as its subject ('[the ravens] were at the ravine of Kisanya') — the sentence's grammar does not settle which is meant, and we do not choose between them.

sentences.t: И ркоша бояре Князю: уже Княже туга умь полонила; се бо два сокола слѣтѣста съ отня стола злата, поискати града Тьмутороканя, а любо испити шеломомь Дону.
sentences.tr: I rkoša bojare Knjazju: uže Knjaže tuga umĭ polonila; se bo dva sokola slětěsta sŭ otnja stola zlata, poiskati grada Tĭmutorokanja, a ljubo ispiti šelomomĭ Donu.
sentences.l: And the boyars said to the prince: ‘Already, Prince, sorrow has taken the mind captive; for two falcons flew down from their father's golden throne, to seek out the city of Tmutorokan, or else to drink of the Don with a helmet.’
sentences.i: And the boyars said to the prince: ‘Already, O Prince, grief has enslaved our minds — for two falcons have flown down from their father's golden throne to seek the city of Tmutorokan, or else to drink the Don from a helmet.’
sentences.n: The boyars now interpret Svyatoslav's dream for him. «два сокола», 'two falcons,' are Igor and Vsevolod; «съ отня стола злата», 'from their father's golden throne,' recalls their late father, and «поискати града Тьмутороканя» echoes the old, half-legendary Rus' hold on Tmutorokan (last securely held by Oleg Svyatoslavich, Igor's grandfather — cf. parts 3–4) that Igor's campaign implicitly tried to reassert. «испити шеломомь Дону», 'to drink the Don with a helmet,' repeats word for word Igor's own vow from part 1 — the boyars now quote his own boast back to him as the disaster it became. слѣтѣста is a dual aorist ('the two flew down'), keeping the paired image of the brothers grammatically visible.

sentences.t: Уже соколома крильца припѣшали поганыхъ саблями, а самаю опустоша въ путины желѣзны.
sentences.tr: Uže sokoloma krilĭca pripěšali poganyxŭ sabljami, a samaju opustoša vŭ putiny želězny.
sentences.l: ‘Already the two falcons' little wings have been pinioned by pagan sabers, and the two of them themselves have been emptied into iron fetters.’
sentences.i: ‘Already pagan sabers have clipped the two falcons' wings, and the two of them have been cast down into iron shackles.’
sentences.n: соколома and самаю are dual forms (dative and accusative respectively) — still tracking Igor and Vsevolod as a pair. припѣшали, 'were pinioned/hobbled' (sharing a root with пута, 'fetters,' echoed a few words later in путины), and опустоша, 'were emptied out, laid waste,' describe the brothers' actual historical capture at the Kayala in plain, brutal terms: the strength that let a falcon fly is disabled, and the men themselves reduced to captives in iron.

sentences.t: Темно бо бѣ въ г̃ день: два солнца помѣркоста, оба багряная стлъпа погасоста, и съ нимъ молодая мѣсяца, Олегъ и Святъславъ тъмою ся поволокоста.
sentences.tr: Temno bo bě vŭ g̃ denĭ: dva solnca poměrkosta, oba bagrjanaja stlŭpa pogasosta, i sŭ nimŭ molodaja měsjaca, Olegŭ i Svjatŭslavŭ tŭmoju sja povolokosta.
sentences.l: For it was dark on the third day: two suns grew dim, both purple pillars went out, and with him, the two young moons, Oleg and Svyatoslav, wrapped themselves in darkness.
sentences.i: For darkness fell on the third day: two suns dimmed, both crimson pillars went dark, and with them the two young moons — Oleg and Svyatoslav — were swallowed up in gloom.
sentences.n: г̃ is a letter under a titlo used as a numeral (here 'three,' 'on the third day'), kept exactly as printed rather than spelled out — compare part 2's д̃, 'four.' The 'two suns' and 'two purple pillars' are usually taken as Igor and Vsevolod (the 'two falcons' named just above); the 'two young moons, Oleg and Svyatoslav,' would then be further kinsmen sharing their captivity — most plausibly Svyatoslav Olgovich of Rylsk, Igor's nephew, who did take part in the 1185 campaign per the Hypatian Chronicle — but the identity of this particular 'Oleg' is not certain, and we do not claim more precision than the text supports. нимъ is a plain singular instrumental ('with him/it') where a dual form (нима) might be expected for two antecedents — a grammatical looseness we note rather than silently regularize. помѣркоста, погасоста, поволокоста are dual aorists throughout, keeping the paired imagery grammatically consistent even where нимъ does not.

sentences.t: На рѣцѣ на Каялѣ тьма свѣтъ покрыла: по Руской земли прострошася Половци, аки пардуже гнѣздо, и въ морѣ погрузиста, и великое буйство подасть Хинови.
sentences.tr: Na rěcě na Kajalě tĭma světŭ pokryla: po Ruskoj zemli prostrošasja Polovci, aki parduže gnězdo, i vŭ morě pogruzista, i velikoe bujstvo podastĭ Xinovi.
sentences.l: On the river, on the Kayala, darkness covered the light: across the Russian land the Polovtsians spread themselves out, like a leopard's brood, and the two of them sank into the sea, and great violence was delivered to Khinova.
sentences.i: On the river Kayala darkness swallowed the light: the Polovtsians spread across the Russian land like a brood of leopards, and the two brothers sank away into the sea, while great havoc broke loose as far as distant Khinova.
sentences.n: Каялѣ, the river Kayala, is again the site of Igor's defeat; as elsewhere in the poem its identity on the modern map is unresolved. «аки пардуже гнѣздо», 'like a leopard's nest/brood,' is a striking simile for how swiftly and savagely the Polovtsians overran the land. погрузиста is a dual aorist ('the two of them sank'), presumably Igor and Vsevolod again, continuing the drowning-in-darkness image from the previous unit. Хинови, 'to the Khins/Khinova,' names a distant, half-legendary people or land (the same Хинова recurs in part 6, «многи страны Хинова»); who exactly is meant — a memory of the Huns, a poetic name for some far-off Asian people, or something else — is not settled. подасть буйство, 'delivers/renders great violence [to them],' is itself unclear in sense (does the disaster's shock reach as far as Khinova, or is 'great violence' something visited on it?); we keep the literal wording and flag the uncertainty rather than resolve it with false confidence.

sentences.t: Уже снесеся хула на хвалу; уже тресну нужда на волю; уже връжеса дивь на землю.
sentences.tr: Uže snesesja xula na xvalu; uže tresnu nužda na volju; uže vrŭžesja divĭ na zemlju.
sentences.l: Already reproach has come down upon praise; already compulsion has burst upon freedom; already the Div has flung itself down upon the earth.
sentences.i: Already shame has swallowed up glory; already bondage has broken in upon freedom; already the Div itself has crashed down to earth.
sentences.n: Three parallel уже-clauses (echoing the same anaphoric уже running through part 4) sum up the reversal: praise turned to reproach, freedom to compulsion. дивь, 'the Div,' is the same ominous demon-bird met crying from the treetop in part 1, warning distant lands of Igor's march while he still rode toward what seemed triumph; its fall to earth here — връжеса, reflexive aorist, 'flung/hurled itself down' — mirrors the collapse of the whole campaign, from a creature that once soared and warned to one brought down.

sentences.t: Се бо Готскія красныя дѣвы въспѣша на брезѣ синему морю.
sentences.tr: Se bo Gotskija krasnyja děvy vŭspěša na brezě sinemu morju.
sentences.l: For, behold, the Gothic fair maidens sang out on the shore by the blue sea.
sentences.i: For now the fair Gothic maidens have broken into song on the shore of the blue sea.
sentences.n: Готскія дѣвы, 'Gothic maidens,' are the Crimean Goths — a genuine, historically attested remnant population descended from the Ostrogoths who stayed on in the Crimea long after the main Gothic migrations (their language, Crimean Gothic, is independently recorded as late as the 16th century). In the poem's own time they were likely allied with, or at least living among, the Polovtsians on the Black Sea coast, and are pictured here as spectators and beneficiaries of the Rus' defeat rather than combatants in it.

sentences.t: Звоня Рускымъ златомъ, поютъ время Бусово, лелѣютъ месть Шароканю.
sentences.tr: Zvonja Ruskymŭ zlatomŭ, pojutŭ vremja Busovo, lelějutŭ mestĭ Šarokanju.
sentences.l: Ringing with Russian gold, they sing of Bus's time, they cherish vengeance for Sharokan.
sentences.i: Jingling with Russian gold, they sing of the age of Bus, nursing their revenge for Sharokan.
sentences.n: звоня Рускымъ златомъ, 'ringing/jingling with Russian gold,' pictures the Goth maidens wearing or handling plunder taken from the Rus'. Бусово время, 'the time of Bus,' is one of the poem's deepest obscurities: one long-standing hypothesis connects Бусъ to 'Boz,' a 4th-century Antian king whom the Gothic historian Jordanes says was crucified by the Ostrogothic king Vinitharius around 375 — if so, the Gothic maidens would be recalling an ancient Gothic triumph over the Slavs' ancestors in the same gloating breath as this new one; but the identification is only proposed, not certain, and we flag it as such rather than assert it. Шароканъ (Sharokan/Sharukan) is a genuine, chronicled Polovtsian khan defeated by Vladimir Monomakh in a series of early-12th-century campaigns; his grandson Konchak was among the khans who defeated Igor in 1185, so 'cherishing vengeance for Sharokan' reads as a generations-long Polovtsian revenge finally realized — one of this passage's few solid historical anchors amid its darker places.

sentences.t: А мы уже дружина жадни веселія.
sentences.tr: A my uže družina žadni veselija.
sentences.l: And we, o retinue, already are hungry for gladness.
sentences.i: And we, my companions, are famished now for any gladness at all.
sentences.n: The poet's own voice breaks in briefly, addressing дружина (as братие is addressed elsewhere) — the retinue or companions, here most likely the poet's own listening audience rather than a prince's war-band. жадни, 'hungry, starved for' (+ gen. веселія), echoes the drooping-gladness image that closed part 4 (веселіе пониче) — joy remains just out of reach.

sentences.t: Тогда Великій Святславъ изрони злато слово слезами смѣшено, и рече: о моя сыновчя Игорю и Всеволоде! рано еста начала Половецкую землю мечи цвѣлити, а себѣ славы искати.
sentences.tr: Togda Velikij Svjatslavŭ izroni zlato slovo slezami směšeno, i reče: o moja synovčja Igorju i Vsevolode! rano esta načala Poloveckuju zemlju meči cvěliti, a sebě slavy iskati.
sentences.l: Then Great Svyatoslav let fall a golden word mixed with tears, and said: ‘O my nephews, Igor and Vsevolod! Early have the two of you begun to trouble the Polovtsian land with swords, and to seek glory for yourselves.’
sentences.i: Then Great Svyatoslav let fall a golden word, mixed with tears, and said: ‘O my kinsmen, Igor and Vsevolod! Too soon did the two of you set out to trouble the Polovtsian land with your swords, and to seek glory for yourselves alone.’
sentences.n: This opens the famous 'Golden Word' (злато слово) — the movement's title-phrase and one of the poem's most celebrated passages, continuing directly into part 6. Святславъ is spelled here without the ъ after т that appears elsewhere in this same part (Святъславь, Святъславъ) — one more small orthographic inconsistency of the 1800 print itself, kept as printed rather than regularized. сыновчя, 'nephews' (sons of a brother), is Svyatoslav's term of address for Igor and Vsevolod; genealogically the three were closer to first cousins — Svyatoslav III's father, Vsevolod Olgovich, and Igor's father, Svyatoslav Olgovich, were themselves brothers, both sons of Oleg Svyatoslavich — but Svyatoslav III, as senior Kievan prince, addresses his younger kinsmen with the more paternal 'nephew.' еста ... начала is a periphrastic dual perfect: еста is the 2nd dual present of быти ('you two are/have'), and начала is the dual masculine l-participle ('[the two of you] began') — together 'the two of you have begun,' preserving the dual number (as with есвѣ in part 1) for exactly the two brothers addressed.

sentences.t: Нъ нечестно одолѣсте: нечестно бо кровь поганую проліясте.
sentences.tr: Nŭ nečestno odolěste: nečestno bo krovĭ poganuju prolijaste.
sentences.l: ‘But dishonorably did you prevail: for dishonorably did you spill pagan blood.’
sentences.i: ‘But you triumphed without honor — for without honor did you spill the pagans' blood.’
sentences.n: одолѣсте and проліясте both carry the ending -сте, which is properly the 2nd person plural aorist ending (cf. рекосте elsewhere in the poem), even though only two people, Igor and Vsevolod, are being addressed — unlike еста just above, a genuine 2nd dual present form. The poem is not perfectly consistent about the dual here: еста marks the pair correctly, but these two aorists use the plural ending for the same two men — a small, real sign of the dual number's gradual collapse into the plural, visible within this very passage rather than asserted from outside it. Svyatoslav's reproach recalls the brothers' initial victory over a Polovtsian detachment (part 2 of the poem), won, in his view, without proper honor or coordination.

sentences.t: Ваю храбрая сердца въ жестоцемъ харалузѣ скована, а въ буести закалена.
sentences.tr: Vaju xrabraja serdca vŭ žestocemŭ xaraluzě skovana, a vŭ buesti zakalena.
sentences.l: ‘Your two brave hearts are forged in stern kharalug, and tempered in ferocity.’
sentences.i: ‘Your brave hearts were forged in hard kharalug steel, and tempered in sheer ferocity.’
sentences.n: Ваю is the true dual genitive/possessive, 'of you two, your (both)' (cf. part 1's Святъславличя for the same dual pattern). скована and закалена are past passive participles picturing the brothers' hearts as smith-work — forged and tempered like the legendary харалугъ steel met throughout the poem (parts 2–4). Real courage is not in doubt here, which is what makes Svyatoslav's reproach land as tragedy rather than simple blame: the fault he names is not cowardice but recklessness.

sentences.t: Се ли створисте моей сребреней сѣдинѣ!
sentences.tr: Se li stvoriste moej srebrenej sědině!
sentences.l: ‘Is this what you have wrought upon my silvered grey hair!’
sentences.i: ‘So this is what you have brought upon my grey head!’
sentences.n: The reproach speech breaks off here at the end of part 5 and continues directly into part 6. створисте again carries the plural aorist ending (see unit 13) addressed to the two brothers. сребреней сѣдинѣ, 'silvered/silver-grey hair,' stands for Svyatoslav's own old age — his grief here is not only political but personal, an old man's lament over what his younger kinsmen have brought down on him.

glossary.аки: аки — like, as (conj.; a spelling variant of акы met in earlier parts)
glossary.багряная: багряный — purple, crimson (dual, agreeing with стлъпа)
glossary.болони: болонь — water-meadow, pasture outside the town walls (loc. sg.)
glossary.босуви: бусыи / Бусовъ — 'dun, grey' (adj.) or possibly 'Bus's' (possessive); disputed reading, see note (nom. pl., agreeing with врани)
glossary.буйство: буйство — violence, wild force, tumult (nom. sg.)
glossary.бусово: Бусъ — Bus's (possessive adj., acc. sg., agreeing with время); an obscure name, see note
glossary.бѣша: быти — there was (an old plural form of быти used impersonally here with the singular дебрь; a grammatical looseness we note rather than resolve)
glossary.ваю: вы — of/for you two, your (gen./dat. dual)
glossary.великое: великый — great (nom. sg. neut., agreeing with буйство)
glossary.великый: великый — great (acc. sg. masc., agreeing with женчюгь; accusative = nominative for inanimate nouns)
glossary.великій: великый — Great (nom. sg. masc., epithet of Svyatoslav); spelled with і here rather than the -ый seen elsewhere in the poem
glossary.веселія: веселие — gladness, joy (gen. sg., object of жадни)
glossary.вмоемъ: въ + мой — in my (prep. + loc. sg. masc.; printed run together as one word in the 1800 edition, kept as printed)
glossary.връжеса: врѣщи (ся) — flung itself, hurled itself down (aorist 3sg, reflexive)
glossary.всю: весь — all, the whole (acc. sg. fem., agreeing with нощь)
glossary.г̃: (numeral 'three,' три — the letter г under a titlo used as a number)
glossary.готскія: Готьскый — Gothic (nom. pl. fem., agreeing with дѣвы); of the Crimean Goths
glossary.два: дъва — two (num., masc.; governs the dual nouns сокола, солнца)
glossary.дивь: дивъ — Div (nom. sg.); the same ominous demon-bird met in part 1
glossary.дону: Донъ — the Don (gen. sg.); the river
glossary.дружина: дружина — druzhina, retinue, companions (voc./nom. sg., collective address)
